headings.title: Introduction and Epidemiology of Lassa Fever in Nigeria
headings.content: Lassa fever is an acute viral haemorrhagic illness that poses a significant public health challenge in Nigeria, with endemic transmission occurring across multiple states, particularly during the dry season. First discovered in the town of Lassa in Borno State, Nigeria, in 1969, the disease is caused by the Lassa virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. Nigeria experiences seasonal outbreaks annually, driven by environmental factors, agricultural practices, and human-rodent interaction. For student nurses preparing for professional examinations in Nigeria, understanding the epidemiology of Lassa fever is crucial for recognizing regional risk patterns and implementing timely public health interventions. The virus is primarily zoonotic, meaning it jumps from animals to humans, though secondary human-to-human transmission is a major concern in healthcare and household settings. Vulnerable populations include residents of rural farming communities, individuals living in housing structures that permit rodent infestation, and healthcare workers who do not strictly adhere to standard infection prevention and control precautions. Mortality rates are generally low overall—around 1%—but can surge dramatically among hospitalized patients with severe clinical presentations, pregnant women in their third trimester, and fetuses, often resulting in maternal and neonatal loss. Surveillance data from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) highlights the continuous need for heightened clinical suspicion, rapid diagnostic testing, and aggressive public health education to curb transmission dynamics and reduce preventable morbidity and mortality nationwide.

headings.title: Aetiology and Vector: The Role of the Mastomys Rat
headings.content: The causative agent of Lassa fever is the Lassa virus, an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Arenaviridae family. The primary natural reservoir and vector for this pathogen is the 'Mastomys natalensis' rat, commonly known as the Natal multimammate mouse or rat. These rodents are prolific breeders widely distributed across sub-Saharan Africa, frequently inhabiting human homes, kitchens, and agricultural storage facilities where food grains are kept. Unlike many other animal hosts that succumb to the diseases they carry, Mastomys rats do not fall ill when infected with the Lassa virus; instead, they become chronic carriers, shedding the virus in their urine, droppings, saliva, and blood throughout their lifespan. For nursing students, recognizing the biology and behavior of the Mastomys rat is essential for understanding how the virus enters human environments. The rats often contaminate food items, utensils, and water sources left uncovered in homes. Furthermore, in certain regions, these rats are captured, prepared, and consumed as a delicacy, presenting a direct high-risk exposure route for hunters, food handlers, and consumers. Controlling the reservoir through environmental sanitation, rodent-proofing of homes, proper food storage in sealed containers, and the use of traps or safe rodenticides forms the cornerstone of primary prevention strategies taught in community health nursing.

headings.title: Modes of Transmission and High-Risk Exposure
headings.content: Transmission of the Lassa virus to humans occurs primarily through ingestion or inhalation of materials contaminated with the excreta of infected Mastomys rats. Specifically, individuals become infected by eating food items or drinking water that has been contaminated with rat urine or feces, or by handling and consuming infected rodents. Another significant route of transmission is inhaling microscopic aerosolized particles of infectious rodent urine or saliva during sweeping, cleaning, or processing grains. Direct contact of broken skin or mucous membranes with contaminated dust or surfaces also poses a high risk. Secondary human-to-human transmission is a critical concern in healthcare and household settings, occurring through direct contact with the blood, urine, feces, vomitus, or other body fluids of an infected person. Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) transmission is well-documented when healthcare workers handle patients without proper Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) or fail to practice rigorous hand hygiene during procedures such as venipuncture, wound care, or management of secretions. Additionally, sexual transmission of the Lassa virus has been documented, as the virus can persist in semen for weeks after clinical recovery. Understanding these exposure routes enables nurses to educate communities effectively and implement strict barrier nursing techniques in clinical areas to protect themselves and other patients.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: Upon entering the human body, the Lassa virus targets dendritic cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells, leading to systemic immune dysregulation and widespread vascular damage. The incubation period ranges from 6 to 21 days, after which symptoms typically begin insidiously with a gradual onset of fever, generalized weakness, malaise, and headache. As the disease progresses, patients manifest a multi-systemic illness characterized by severe retro-sternal chest pain, sore throat, myalgia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. In severe cases, increased capillary permeability and endothelial dysfunction lead to hypovolemic shock, pleural effusion, facial edema, and mucosal bleeding (such as epistaxis, hematemesis, or bleeding from puncture sites). Neurological complications, including sensorineural hearing loss, tremors, encephalitis, and seizures, can occur during the acute phase or persist during convalescence. The classic presentation of Lassa fever can easily mimic other endemic febrile illnesses in Nigeria, such as malaria, typhoid fever, and other viral haemorrhagic fevers like yellow fever or Ebola. A hallmark clinical sign that should raise high suspicion in endemic zones is exudative pharyngitis with yellowish-white patches on the tonsils, accompanied by a lack of response to standard anti-malarials and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Nurses must carefully monitor vital signs, fluid balance, and bleeding tendencies to detect early signs of clinical deterioration and impending circulatory collapse.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Nursing assessment and diagnostic evaluation of a suspected Lassa fever patient require a high index of suspicion combined with strict adherence to infection control protocols. When taking a nursing history, nurses must elicit a detailed epidemiological profile, inquiring about travel history to endemic areas, contact with known Lassa fever patients, and evidence of rodent infestation in the patient's home or workplace. Physical assessment involves continuous monitoring of vital signs to detect pyrexia, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnoea, while closely inspecting for signs of bleeding, facial swelling, and dehydration. Diagnostic confirmation relies heavily on laboratory investigations, with the Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) assay being the gold standard for detecting viral RNA in blood or body fluids. Other essential tests include Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) to detect Lassa IgM and IgG antibodies, viral antigen detection tests, and complete blood count (CBC) which frequently reveals leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. Routine urinalysis may show proteinuria. Nurses collecting blood and biological specimens must wear full personal protective equipment (PPE), use leak-proof containers, and label specimens as hazardous to protect laboratory personnel. Prompt communication of preliminary findings to the medical team ensures that supportive care and specific antiviral therapy are initiated without delay.

headings.title: Medical Management and Pharmacological Treatment
headings.content: Medical management of Lassa fever centers on prompt administration of specific antiviral chemotherapy and aggressive supportive care to maintain hemodynamic stability. The antiviral drug of choice is Ribavirin, a synthetic nucleoside analogue that has been proven to significantly reduce morbidity and mortality when administered early in the course of the disease—preferably within the first six days of symptom onset. Ribavirin is typically administered intravenously (IV) in a loading dose followed by maintenance doses over a ten-day regimen, though oral administration can be used in certain outpatient or post-exposure prophylaxis scenarios under strict medical guidance. Supportive medical therapy is equally vital and includes aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia, correction of electrolyte imbalances, blood product transfusions (such as fresh frozen plasma or platelets) for severe bleeding disorders, and management of secondary bacterial infections with appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics. Antipyretics like paracetamol are used for fever control, while medications that impair coagulation, such as aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), must be strictly avoided to prevent exacerbating haemorrhagic manifestations. Patients experiencing acute kidney injury may require renal replacement therapy. Medical and nursing teams must collaborate closely to closely monitor organ function, fluid intake and output, and treatment side effects, particularly Ribavirin-induced hemolytic anaemia, ensuring timely laboratory checks throughout the hospital stay.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Management
headings.content: Developing and executing a comprehensive nursing care plan for a patient with Lassa fever requires a systematic approach focused on physiological stabilization, strict barrier nursing, and psychological support. Key nursing diagnoses often include Risk for Fluid Volume Deficit related to vomiting, diarrhea, and capillary leakage; Ineffective Tissue Perfusion related to hypovolemic shock and vascular endothelial damage; Hyperthermia related to the viral infection; and Anxiety related to social stigma and the severity of the illness. Interventions include maintaining accurate fluid balance charts with hourly urine output measurements via an indwelling catheter, administering prescribed intravenous fluids and Ribavirin on schedule, monitoring vital signs every two to four hours, and providing meticulous skin and oral hygiene to prevent secondary infections. Nurses must implement strict isolation protocols, placing the patient in a designated Lassa fever isolation room or cohort area with restricted visitor access. Psychological support is paramount, as patients and their families often experience profound fear and social isolation due to the stigma attached to viral haemorrhagic fevers. Nurses should offer empathetic communication, reassurance, and clear explanations of procedures. Furthermore, nurses must monitor for complications such as sensorineural hearing loss, providing necessary rehabilitative referrals upon discharge, and educate convalescent patients regarding safe sexual practices, as the virus can persist in semen for several weeks post-recovery.

headings.title: Infection Prevention and Control in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Infection prevention and control (IPC) is the most critical line of defense against nosocomial transmission of Lassa fever in Primary Health Care (PHC) centers across Nigeria. Because Lassa fever often presents with non-specific symptoms in its early stages, PHC nurses must maintain a high index of suspicion and apply standard precautions universally to all patients presenting with febrile illnesses. Standard, contact, and droplet precautions must be rigorously implemented the moment Lassa fever is suspected. Healthcare workers must wear appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), including water-resistant gowns, gloves, surgical masks or N95 respirators, eye protection (face shields or goggles), and waterproof boots when providing direct patient care or handling potentially infectious specimens. Hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub must be performed before and after every patient contact and after removing PPE. Safe injection practices and proper management of sharp instruments are mandatory to prevent needle-stick injuries. Environmental sanitation involves cleaning and disinfecting contaminated surfaces, floors, and medical equipment using hypochlorite solution (chlorine bleach) prepared to recommended concentrations. Furthermore, safe handling and dignified, safe burial of deceased patients whose bodies are highly infectious are essential components of PHC-level infection control to break the chain of transmission within the community.

headings.title: Community Health Education and Disease Surveillance
headings.content: Community health education and active disease surveillance are vital public health functions that empower populations and enable rapid containment of Lassa fever outbreaks in Nigeria. Community health nurses play a pivotal role in designing and executing culturally appropriate health education campaigns aimed at breaking the rodent-human transmission cycle. Key educational messages must emphasize proper food storage in sealed rodent-proof containers, drying food grains on elevated platforms rather than on bare ground or roadsides, refraining from hunting and consuming Mastomys rats, maintaining clean home environments, and seeking prompt medical attention at the nearest health facility upon the onset of fever. Nurses should also work to dispel myths, reduce social stigma associated with the disease, and encourage community members to report suspected cases early. Concurrently, disease surveillance involves systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data to detect disease clusters and monitor epidemiological trends. Nurses at the primary, secondary, and tertiary levels are responsible for immediate case notification and reporting suspected Lassa fever cases up the public health chain to Local Government Area (LGA) disease surveillance and notification officers (DSNOs) and the NCDC. Effective community engagement and robust surveillance systems ensure timely outbreak responses, contact tracing, and community-wide containment measures that save lives.
